documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
54 yo woman establishing care. Prior PCP office downsizing.

Diabetes: told about 6 years ago on routine labs. Metformin 1000 twice a day the whole time, never on insulin or anything else. Doesn't check sugars at home much. Last A1c she remembers was "around 7." No eye or foot problems she knows of. Sees an optometrist yearly.
Hypertension: about 8 years. Lisinopril 20 and HCTZ 12.5, both in the morning. Doesn't own a cuff.
Atorvastatin 20 started by her old doctor "because of the diabetes." No muscle aches.

Other hx: menopause at 52, no hormones ever, no bleeding since. Chickenpox as a kid. Has lost several teeth over the years and had them pulled; partial edentulism, wears nothing currently.
No surgeries otherwise. No known drug allergies.
FH: mother T2DM; father HTN; paternal grandfather heart disease.
SH: retired admin assistant (school district office). Lives alone in Greenfield. Never smoked, no alcohol.
Health maintenance per pt: colonoscopy ~3 yrs ago normal, Pap last year normal, mammogram this past spring. Records requested.

ROS otherwise negative.
Exam: well, pleasant. BP as charted. HEENT: partial edentulism, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, NT. Ext no edema. Feet: skin intact, monofilament intact bilaterally, DP pulses 2+.
PHQ-2 0.

A/P
1. T2DM, on metformin. A1c, UACR today.
2. HTN, at goal today on lisinopril/HCTZ. CMP.
3. Statin for diabetes, continue. Lipids.
4. HM: HCV and HIV screen once today. Flu shot in Oct. Mammo due spring. Colonoscopy and Pap per records.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP

Kidney function, liver tests, blood counts and potassium are all normal, and there is no protein leaking in the urine. LDL is in a good place on the atorvastatin. Hepatitis C and HIV screens were negative. No changes for now, see you in December.

documents.title: Office Visit: Urinary Symptoms
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
57F. Visit set up at the physical to go over bladder symptoms.
HPI: For roughly half a year she has been going far more often, with a strong need to get there fast, and a stinging feeling when she voids even between infections. Two documented UTIs this year. Some small leaks when she can't make it, slowly getting worse. Tried cranberry capsules from the drugstore and pushing water; no difference, if anything more trips. No fever, no hematuria, no flank pain. No vaginal bleeding. Menopause at 52, never on hormones.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, HCTZ, atorvastatin. NKDA.
Exam: chaperoned pelvic. Vulvar skin thin and pale, external genitalia atrophic. Vaginal walls dry with loss of the normal folds. No discharge, no bleeding. Bimanual nontender, no masses.
UA today clean: no LE, nitrite, blood, protein or glucose.
A/P
1. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: fits the dryness, burning and likely the recurrent infections. Start vaginal estradiol cream, 1 g nightly x2 wk then twice weekly. Low dose, local; explained it is not the same as systemic hormone therapy. She is willing.
2. Urgency with leakage: urgency-predominant by history. Referral to urology for evaluation. Meanwhile cut back on caffeine, timed voiding.
3. Recurrent cystitis: as #1; return for dip/culture with any symptoms.
F/u after urology.

documents.title: Urology consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY CONSULTATION, date of visit 02/05/2024
Referred by primary care for urgency with leakage.

Ms. Ellis is a 57-year-old woman whose bladder complaints were first worked up by her PCP in October. Over about half a year she has had abrupt, very strong urges to void, and on some occasions does not get to the toilet in time. This has started to change how she lives; she now thinks twice before being away from home for long. On her own she cut down on coffee and tea and began emptying her bladder on a two-hour clock, without much benefit. On vaginal estrogen since November for atrophy.

PMH: type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, also takes atorvastatin. Postmenopausal. Partial edentulism after dental extractions.
Allergies: none known.
Family: mother diabetes, father hypertension.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, retired.

Exam: abdomen soft, nontender, no masses or suprapubic fullness. Pelvic exam: no prolapse of anterior, apical or posterior compartments; no other abnormality.
Urinalysis: negative for infection, glucose and protein.
Bladder scan post-void residual: 20 mL, normal.

Impression: urge urinary incontinence, urgency predominant, with normal emptying.

Plan:
- 3-day bladder diary.
- Bladder training with gradual lengthening of intervals; urge suppression techniques reviewed.
- Referral to pelvic floor physical therapy.
- Revisit in several months; medication if behavioral measures fail.

Thank you for this referral.

documents.title: Otolaryngology consultation
documents.author: otolaryngology
documents.body:
Otolaryngology — Consultation
DOS: 05/03/2024
Reason: palatal mass, referred by PCP at the request of her dentist.

History: 57-year-old woman with a year of gradually increasing discomfort in the mouth, with some difficulty eating and, at times, trouble getting words out clearly. She has lost several teeth recently and wants dentures, but is worried a denture will not sit properly over this lump. Diabetes and hypertension, both reported as well controlled on her current medicines.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin.
Allergies: NKDA.
Non-smoker, no alcohol.

Examination: In the midline of the hard palate there is a bony-hard, nontender swelling. It does not blanch on pressure. Overlying mucosa is intact with no ulceration. Remainder of the oral cavity and oropharynx unremarkable. No cervical lymphadenopathy.

Impression: torus palatinus, a benign bony overgrowth.

Plan: reassured; no biopsy or imaging needed. Recommend she work with her dentist or a prosthodontist on a denture design that accommodates the torus. If a usable denture cannot be made, surgical reduction can be considered at that point. Return as needed.
Copy to PCP.

documents.title: Urology follow-up
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY FOLLOW-UP — 11/06/2024

58-year-old postmenopausal woman returning for urge incontinence, seen here in February after her PCP's evaluation last October. Despite bladder training, a diary and four pelvic floor PT sessions, things have steadily worsened over roughly eight months. The urge comes on abruptly and without warning, in her words "out of nowhere," and she often leaks a moderate amount before reaching the toilet. This happens several times a day and some nights. Restricting fluids has not changed the urgency. She does not leak with coughing, laughing or exercise. No sense of incomplete emptying, no post-void dribbling. No dysuria, blood in the urine or pelvic pain. She lives on her own and stays active locally, but has started skipping outings for fear of an accident.

PMH: mild hypertension, on a low-dose thiazide plus lisinopril; type 2 diabetes; postmenopausal. No prior pelvic surgery.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, vaginal estradiol.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: pelvic floor tone normal, no prolapse. Neurologic screen normal (perineal sensation, lower extremity strength and reflexes).
UA: negative for leukocyte esterase, nitrite, blood and glucose.

Assessment: refractory urge urinary incontinence after behavioral therapy.
Plan: start mirabegron 25 mg daily (chosen over an anticholinergic at her age). Have PCP watch BP. Continue timed voiding and vaginal estrogen. Follow up in 3 to 4 months, sooner if no benefit.

Thank you.

documents.title: Pulmonology consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PULMONARY CONSULTATION
Visit: 01/20/2025. Requested by PCP for chronic cough.

HPI: Ms. Ellis, 58, has had a dry cough for about three months, which began while she was in the middle of her urology care. It brings up nothing. She is not short of breath and has had no wheezing or chest pain. Never smoker. No reflux symptoms, no nasal drainage. Chest film from December is clear.

PMH: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, urge incontinence, torus palatinus, postmenopausal.
Medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, metformin, atorvastatin, mirabegron, vaginal estradiol.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family: mother diabetes; father hypertension; paternal grandfather heart disease.
Social: never smoked; no alcohol; retired.

Vitals: BP 135/85, HR 78, RR 16.
Exam: no distress. Lungs clear to auscultation, no wheezes, rales or rhonchi. Remainder of exam unremarkable.
Recent labs from PCP (01/10/2025): HbA1c 7.2%, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, potassium 4.5 mEq/L.

Assessment: chronic nonproductive cough with clear lungs and normal chest film in a never-smoker taking an ACE inhibitor. Most likely an adverse effect of lisinopril.
Recommendation: stop lisinopril. Cough from ACE inhibitors usually settles over weeks, occasionally a few months. Would avoid re-challenge. If cough persists 8 to 12 weeks off the drug, happy to see her again for spirometry and further evaluation. Blood pressure management per PCP.

Thank you for the consult.

documents.title: Pulmonology recommendation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt after the pulmonology note came over. They think the cough is from lisinopril. Asked her to stop it starting today and to keep the HCTZ. Added lisinopril to allergies as an intolerance (cough). Please check home BP a few times a week and send me readings in two weeks; we'll see her in March. She was glad to have an answer.

reports.text: CT chest without contrast. Bilateral ground-glass and consolidative opacities, lower-lobe predominant. Small bilateral pleural effusions. No mass. No pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar nodes. Heart size normal, no pericardial effusion. Airways patent.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral lower-lobe predominant ground-glass and consolidative opacities with small effusions.

reports.text: Specimen: bronchoalveolar lavage, right middle lobe, sequential aliquots. Gross: aliquots progressively more blood-tinged. Cytology: numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages; no malignant cells; no viral cytopathic effect. Bacterial, fungal and AFB cultures: no growth.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE — 04/25/2025 15:30
CC: fever, shortness of breath, dry cough x3 days.
HPI: 58F, diabetes, hypertension, urge incontinence, with a pulmonology evaluation for cough earlier this year. Three days of fever, breathlessness and a dry cough. Onset about a week after starting an antibiotic for a bladder infection (TMP-SMX per pharmacy record). No travel, no sick contacts.
Home meds per pharmacy: metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, mirabegron, vaginal estradiol.
Allergies: lisinopril (cough).
VS: T 38.5 C, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 92% RA.
Exam: mildly tachypneic. Crackles at both bases. Diffuse erythematous rash over trunk and upper arms. Heart tachycardic, regular. No leg swelling.
Labs: WBC 12.0 with normal differential, Hgb 13.2, plt 250, Cr 1.0, BUN 14, CRP 50.
CXR: bilateral basilar opacities, small effusions.
ED course: 2 L nasal cannula to SpO2 95%. Blood and urine cultures. Admitted to medicine; pulmonology consulted.
Note: lisinopril appears on pharmacy list though PCP records show it stopped in January; pt confirms she is not taking it.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 04/25/2025, discharged 04/30/2025.

Principal diagnosis: diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, drug-induced (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
Secondary: diffuse rash with the reaction, resolving; type 2 diabetes, glucose elevated on steroids; hypertension; urge incontinence.

Course: Presented with fever, hypoxemia, basilar crackles and a truncal rash a week into TMP-SMX for cystitis. CT chest showed bilateral lower-lobe predominant ground-glass and consolidative change with small effusions. Pulmonology performed bronchoscopy on 4/26; BAL returns grew more bloody with each aliquot and cytology showed hemosiderin-laden macrophages, with negative cultures. Blood and urine cultures negative. TMP-SMX was stopped and listed as an allergy. Treated with IV methylprednisolone for 2 days, then oral prednisone 40 mg daily. Oxygen weaned to room air by 4/28. Rash faded. Metformin held, insulin correction scale used during admission for glucose up to the high 200s on steroids; metformin resumed at discharge.

Discharge exam: afebrile, SpO2 95% on room air at rest and with ambulation, faint basilar crackles, rash fading.

Discharge medications:
- prednisone taper: 40 mg daily x4 days (started 4/27), then 30 mg x4, 20 mg x4, 10 mg x4, then stop
- metformin 1000 mg twice daily
- hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily
- atorvastatin 20 mg daily
- mirabegron 25 mg daily
- estradiol vaginal cream twice weekly
STOP: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Do not take sulfonamide antibiotics.

Allergies: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, rash) — severe; lisinopril (cough).

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; check fingerstick glucose daily while on prednisone. Pulmonology clinic in 6 weeks with chest x-ray.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Transition call, discharged 4/30. Breathing better, walking around the house without getting winded. No fever. On prednisone 40 daily, switches to 30 on 5/1 per her calendar. Fingersticks 180s to 220s since starting prednisone. Med list reconciled against the discharge summary; TMP-SMX allergy entered. Appointment 5/5 confirmed.

documents.title: Post-discharge Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after admission 4/25-4/30 for drug-induced diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from TMP-SMX. Discharge summary, CT and BAL results reviewed.
Now: breathing close to normal, light dry cough now and then, no hemoptysis, no fever. Rash almost gone. Bladder symptoms resolved. On prednisone 30 mg today in the taper. Home sugars 170s to 210s, expected on steroids; no symptoms of high sugar.
Exam: comfortable. SpO2 normal on RA. Lungs: few fine crackles at the right base only. Skin: faint fading macular erythema on upper back. No edema.
A/P
1. DAH from TMP-SMX: improving. Finish taper. Pulm follow-up in June with CXR. TMP-SMX and sulfonamide antibiotics never again; flagged in chart.
2. Steroid hyperglycemia on T2DM: continue metformin, log sugars; should settle after the taper.
3. Cystitis: resolved, culture-proven, treated.
4. HTN: HCTZ.
BMP today.

PULMONARY FOLLOW-UP — 06/10/2025
Seen after April admission for TMP-SMX-induced diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, treated with drug withdrawal and corticosteroids.
She feels back to normal: no cough, no shortness of breath, no hemoptysis. Steroid taper finished 5/12.
Allergies: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (alveolar hemorrhage), lisinopril (cough).
SpO2 97% RA. Lungs clear throughout.
CXR today: prior opacities and effusions resolved.
Impression: diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, resolved.
Plan: lifelong avoidance of TMP-SMX. No further pulmonary follow-up needed; return if new respiratory symptoms.
Thank you.

Dermatology — 10/24/2025
Same-day referral from primary care.
HPI: 59-year-old woman with a painful eruption on the left flank for three days. The pain, a steady burning, started several days before any rash. Had chickenpox in childhood. No prior shingles vaccine.
PMH: type 2 diabetes and hypertension, reported well controlled. Meds: metformin, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, mirabegron, vaginal estradiol.
Allergies: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (alveolar hemorrhage), lisinopril (cough).
Vitals: T 37.2 C, BP 132/84, HR 78.
Exam: grouped clear vesicles on an erythematous base in a band following the left T8 dermatome, stopping at the midline. Remainder of skin exam unremarkable.
Recent PCP labs (10/08/2025): CBC within normal limits, fasting glucose 146 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.2%.
Impression: herpes zoster, left T8.
Plan: valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days. Acetaminophen for pain. Keep lesions covered until crusted. Recombinant zoster vaccine once healed, through PCP. Return if spreading or eye symptoms.

documents.title: Emergency department note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
ED PROVIDER NOTE — 05/01/2026
CC: burning pain left chest for 3 days.
HPI: 59F with shingles of the left mid-torso about six months ago. For three days a constant burning pain has been back on the left side of her chest wall, wrapping toward the back in the same area. No injury. No exertional component, no shortness of breath, no diaphoresis.
PMH: T2DM, HTN, urge incontinence, prior drug-induced alveolar hemorrhage.
Meds: metformin, HCTZ, atorvastatin, mirabegron, vaginal estradiol; lisinopril listed on outside list, pt says stopped last year.
Allergies: TMP-SMX (alveolar hemorrhage), lisinopril (cough).
Vitals: within normal limits.
Exam: heart regular, lungs clear. Left chest wall: increased sensitivity to light touch over the band where the zoster was; skin intact, no rash or vesicles.
ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no ischemic changes. hs-Troponin I 3 ng/L.
MDM: cardiac cause unlikely with normal ECG and troponin and a pain pattern matching the old dermatome. Pain in the prior T8 zoster distribution, neuropathic.
Disposition: home. Gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime; acetaminophen as needed. PCP follow-up this week. Return for chest pressure, breathlessness or new rash.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED visit 5/1 reviewed: burning left chest wall pain in the old shingles band, no rash, ECG and troponin normal, sent home on gabapentin 300 qhs.
Today: pain somewhat better, sleeping through the night. Mild grogginess in the morning the first two days, now gone. No rash has appeared.
Exam: skin intact over left T8, mild allodynia. Lungs clear, heart regular.
A/P: neuropathic pain at the prior zoster site. Continue gabapentin 300 at bedtime; may stop once pain-free for a few weeks, check with me first. Has had both Shingrix doses. Note for chart: lisinopril still appears on some outside lists; it is not an active medication.
